brief: Deutsche Bank frames the global bond sell-off as continued normalisation, not stress. US 10yr yields sit only slightly above the 4.5% average since 1800, and with nominal GDP at 6.6% the gap to 10yr yields is about 180bps, so yields are hard to call too high. If nominal GDP settles at 5.5% then 4.8% is average, at 6% on AI and inflation about 5.3% is reasonable before fiscal concerns. Across developed markets funding costs now exceed nominal GDP, with France, Italy and the UK most negative. On the Fed, core PCE is 15bps off a 34-year high, trend inflation is sticky near 3%, financial conditions are the loosest since 1990, policy sits below rules and payrolls have turned up in 2026, so the 2025 insurance cuts look ripe to be reversed. For the ECB, the energy shock pushed the real deposit rate negative and markets price 75bps more hikes. DB economists expect a hike this week and another to 2.75% in December. Q2 delivered the strongest non-pandemic global earnings growth on record, driven by an AI capex boom where the top five spenders outspend the other 495. The yen is off 40-year lows after 15.4tn yen of intervention.
